implementation_notes: pygame ships the pattern's hook and collection: Sprite.update is 'a convenient "hook" that you can override' and Group.update 'Calls the update() method on all Sprites in the Group', passing the same arguments to every member - the group is the collection and the call is the driver. What replaces the classic structure: Sprite replaces the entity base class and Group replaces the entity manager, so an update(dt) method per sprite plus one group call per frame is the whole pattern. Outside pygame the same shape works with duck typing - any object with update(dt) and a plain list loop - which is the version to use in headless simulations and non-pygame applications; a hand-written base class is only justified when entities share bookkeeping such as position, velocity or sprite images.
code_sketch:
class Guard(pygame.sprite.Sprite):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.x = 0.0
    def update(self, dt):                       # the hook
        self.x += 20.0 * dt

guards = pygame.sprite.Group(Guard())
# in the frame loop:
guards.update(dt)                               # walks every sprite
pitfalls: Group.update passes the same arguments to every sprite, so per-object parameters must live on the sprite; a group whose members disagree on the signature fails at the first mismatched member.
Adding or killing sprites inside update mutates the group while it is being walked - kill() and the group's internal set are the tools, and removals should be batched after the walk.

Python-level update methods plus attribute access are the bottleneck at thousands of objects and the GIL blocks parallel stepping: profile before scaling, and consider array-based/SoA representations for bulk behaviour.
The base Sprite.update accepts any arguments and does nothing, so a misspelled method name silently updates nothing - override explicitly and keep a smoke test for each updatable kind.
